comparator.name: Circular Engineering
comparator.sourceNotes: The official document titled 2026–27, dated August 2026, and the programme curriculum are the basis for this illustration. Articles 3.5–3.9 and Appendix I set out three 60 EC years. The cover and Appendix describe the current published curriculum, while Articles 1.1 and 8.4 retain 2025–26 dates. The Year 2 electives illustrate two courses and one skill per teaching period, subject to availability and academic advice. Article 3.8 describes a concentration-linked skills requirement, while Appendix I labels Heat & Mass Transfer as the linked course and lists Analytical and Physical Chemistry Skills separately. The example retains those options as illustrative and does not assert that the skills choice has been formally approved. The selected Circular Chemical Engineering concentration follows the published order. The 25 EC individual thesis requires 120 EC overall, including 60 EC from Year 1 and at least 40 EC from Year 2.

alternativeSelection.assessment: Two coherent responses materially engage with circular product and resource design, and with the biological foundations and environmental application of sustainable production. The first includes prototyping, lifecycle assessment, recovery experiments and renewable-system design. The second develops biological, ecological and laboratory depth alongside circular production. The mechanical and manufacturing direction was tested against robotics, mathematical modelling and product design. These provide meaningful partial applications but do not sustain mechanical design, instrumentation, materials production or fabrication as the main field of study.

comparisonAlignment.rationale: Both address circular and sustainable systems; UCR supplies sustainability foundations rather than engineering fundamentals.
Both centre life-cycle assessment; the UCR course analyses products and processes but is not an engineering design project.
Both include analytical work on chemical and material systems; UCR focuses on environmental geochemistry and resource recovery rather than physical-chemistry engineering skills.
Both study how products and materials can be kept in use. UCR develops recovery and remediation methods through laboratory work.
UCR develops molecular and cellular foundations for biotechnology. Maastricht applies these foundations to engineering and production.
Both directly teach biochemistry, while UCR situates it within life science rather than chemical engineering.
Both include biology laboratory work; UCR offers one broad life-science laboratory rather than combined chemistry-and-engineering practical training.
Both provide calculus foundations; UCR Mathematical Methods is a broader science course rather than engineering mathematics.
Both develop statistics for scientific analysis.
Both directly teach computational and numerical methods for scientific problems.
Both directly teach linear algebra.
Both develop multivariable calculus; UCR also includes differential equations.
UCR has no fundamentals-of-engineering course.
UCR has no chemistry-and-chemical-engineering foundation.
UCR has no thermodynamics-and-engineering-physics course.
UCR sustainability study does not reproduce engineering skills training.
UCR has no physics-and-electronics laboratory sequence.
Both use a design project to connect specifications to a practical solution. UCR focuses on consumer products and prototypes, while Maastricht applies engineering methods in a design sequence.
UCR has no organic chemistry course.
UCR has no fluid mechanics course.
UCR has no polymeric-materials engineering course.
UCR mathematics includes differential equations but not this engineering elective structure.
UCR has no heat-and-mass-transfer course.
UCR has no organic-chemistry skills course.

notes.text: Both UCR options offer work in circularity and environmental science. The first focuses on materials recovery and product design. The second focuses on life science and sustainable production.

Maastricht’s selected concentration develops thermodynamics, reactor and plant design, and process control, and concludes with a 25 EC engineering thesis. UCR offers related laboratory, design and modelling work with a different scope.

audience.programmeDescription: Maastricht’s Circular Engineering bachelor combines mathematics, natural sciences and engineering design to develop lower-impact products and processes. This example follows Circular Chemical Engineering.
audience.comparisonExplanation: The UCR options offer related work in circular design, environmental systems and sustainable production. The Maastricht example follows the document headed 2026–2027. Its effective-date clauses still refer to 2025–2026. The Year 2 elective example is subject to availability and academic advice.

cellNotes.text: Both address circular and sustainable systems; UCR supplies sustainability foundations rather than engineering fundamentals.
